power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

table.title: Intersectional inequalities in demand satisfied by modern contraceptive methods among women in sub-Saharan Africa, 1992 to 2024: a multilevel analysis of individual heterogeneity and discriminatory accuracy
table.research_questions: RQ1. How does demand satisfied by modern methods vary across intersectional strata defined by age, marital status, education, household wealth and place of residence among women in sub-Saharan Africa? RQ2. How much of the individual variation in demand satisfied lies between intersectional strata, and how well do the strata discriminate between women whose demand is and is not satisfied? RQ3. How much of the between-stratum variation is explained by additive effects, and which strata differ from what the additive effects predict? RQ4. How have intersectional inequalities changed between 1992 and 2024, and which strata caught up, stayed behind or fell further behind? RQ5. How do intersectional inequalities differ between countries and sub-regions? RQ6. Which strata were persistently left behind across all periods? H1. Demand satisfied will vary across strata, with the lowest levels among adolescent, unmarried, poorer, rural women with no schooling. H2. The strata will have low to moderate discriminatory accuracy, with a variance partition coefficient (VPC) below 20% and an AUC below 0.70. H3. Additive main effects will explain more than 80% of the between-stratum variance (PCV above 80%), but some strata will show interaction effects whose 95% intervals exclude zero. H4. The between-stratum variance will be smaller in 2018 to 2024 than in 1992 to 1999, but strata combining adolescence, no schooling and rural residence will have improved least. H5. Intersectional inequalities will be wider in West and Central Africa than in East and Southern Africa. All hypotheses are evaluated within a frequentist multilevel framework using 95% confidence intervals, with Bayesian models as sensitivity analyses. Rationale: intersectionality theory and earlier single-dimension DHS studies showing lower demand satisfied among adolescents, unmarried, poorer, rural and less educated women.
table.datasets_used: Women's individual recode (IR) files of standard Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS) conducted in sub-Saharan African countries with fieldwork from 1992 to 2024. Subset: women aged 15 to 49 years with demand for family planning (v626a coded 1 to 4). Interim, special, malaria indicator, AIDS indicator and subnational surveys are excluded.
table.data_access: The data are not openly downloadable. They are freely available to registered researchers after the DHS Program approves a project request.
table.access_date: The DHS Program approved access for this project on 19 October 2026 for 41 countries and one subnational survey (Angola, Benin, Botswana, Burkina Faso, Burundi, Cameroon, Central African Republic, Chad, Comoros, Congo, Congo Democratic Republic, Cote d'Ivoire, Eritrea, Eswatini, Ethiopia, Gabon, Gambia, Ghana, Guinea, Kenya, Lesotho, Liberia, Madagascar, Malawi, Mali, Mauritania, Mozambique, Namibia, Niger, Nigeria, Nigeria Ondo State, Rwanda, Sao Tome and Principe, Senegal, Sierra Leone, South Africa, Sudan, Tanzania, Togo, Uganda, Zambia, Zimbabwe). At the time of registration, no data for this project had been downloaded by any author. Data will be downloaded after this registration is submitted.
table.data_collection_procedures: DHS surveys are nationally representative household surveys using two-stage stratified cluster sampling, with standard questionnaires administered face to face by trained interviewers. Possible biases include self-reported contraceptive use, under-reporting among unmarried women, survey non-response, and changes in questionnaire phases over time. The revised DHS unmet need definition is applied consistently to all surveys.
table.codebook: DHS recode manuals for each phase (DHS-II to DHS-8) and the Guide to DHS Statistics (Croft et al., 2018). Most relevant: the definitions of unmet need (v626a), current method type (v313), and the background variables v013, v502, v106, v190 and v025.
table.measured_variables: Outcome: demand satisfied by modern methods, coded 1 if a woman with demand for family planning uses a modern method (v313 = 3) and 0 otherwise. Stratification dimensions: age (v013) as 15 to 19, 20 to 24, 25 to 34, 35 to 49; marital status (v502) as in union or not in union; education (v106) as none, primary, secondary or higher; wealth (v190) as poorest 40%, middle 20%, richest 40%; residence (v025) as urban or rural. These form 144 intersectional strata. Contextual variables: survey (v000, v007), period (1992 to 1999, 2000 to 2009, 2010 to 2017, 2018 to 2024), country, and sub-region (West and Central Africa, East and Southern Africa, UNICEF grouping). Design variables: v005, v021, v022. Sensitivity variable: parity (v201) as 0, 1 to 2, 3 or more.
table.missing_data_handling: Missingness in DHS outcome and background variables is expected to be under 2%. Women missing the outcome or any stratification variable will be excluded, and exclusions reported by survey. If more than 5% of eligible women are excluded in any survey, multiple imputation by chained equations with 20 imputations will be used as a sensitivity analysis.
table.sampling_weights: Weights (v005) are available. Descriptive estimates will be weighted and account for clustering and stratification, with weights rescaled so that each survey contributes equally to pooled estimates. Main multilevel models will be unweighted, because standard weighting can bias variance components; survey is included as a random effect. Weighted multilevel models with scaled weights will be a sensitivity analysis.
table.prior_publication_dissemination: Patrick Kaonga has analysed Zambia DHS data (2007, 2013-14, 2018 and 2024) in other papers, including work on contraceptive method mix, discontinuation and unmet need. Sylvia Masambi, Musopa Nkole and Isaac Fwemba co-author the Zambia contraceptive method mix and discontinuation paper. No author has published an intersectional or MAIHDA analysis of demand satisfied using DHS data from any country
table.prior_knowledge: The authors know published national estimates of demand satisfied from DHS final reports and from Zambia DHS analyses, and the literature showing single-dimension inequalities. No author has examined demand satisfied by intersectional strata, or analysed the IR files of the other 38 countries for this question. The hypotheses are based on published literature, not on prior analysis of these data.
table.statistical_tests: Multilevel logistic regression with women nested in intersectional strata, with survey as a cross-classified random effect. Model 1, null: stratum and survey random intercepts (VPC, AUC; H1, H2). Model 2, additive: Model 1 plus main effects of the five dimensions (PCV and stratum interaction effects; H3). Model 3: Model 2 plus period. Model 4: Models 1 and 2 by period (H4, VPC and PCV change). Model 5: Models 1 and 2 by sub-region (H5). Model 6: Model 2 plus period with stratum and stratum × period random effects (stratum trajectories; H4). Model 7: Model 2 plus period with stratum and stratum × country random effects (country variation; H5). VPC = σ²u / (σ²u + σ²s + π²/3). PCV = (σ²u1 − σ²u2) / σ²u1. Estimated in Stata 18 with melogit (adaptive quadrature).
table.effect_size: This is an estimation study. Quantities of interest are the VPC, PCV, AUC, stratum-specific predicted probabilities, stratum interaction effects (odds ratios) and changes in predicted demand satisfied in percentage points. A difference of 5 percentage points in predicted demand satisfied between periods or strata is considered programmatically meaningful.
table.statistical_power: With over one million women and 144 strata, the median stratum is expected to contain several thousand women, giving 95% intervals for stratum estimates of about ±2 percentage points. Strata with fewer than 30 women will be retained but flagged.
table.inference_criteria: 95% confidence intervals. A stratum interaction effect is considered present if its 95% interval excludes zero. Strata are classified as catching up or falling behind if their change differs from the overall average change and the 95% interval excludes the average. Multilevel shrinkage reduces false positives across the 144 strata, and all stratum results will be reported, not only those that are significant. AUC is interpreted as below 0.60 absent or poor, 0.60 to 0.70 small, 0.70 to 0.80 moderate, above 0.80 large. A persistently left behind stratum is one in the lowest 10% of predicted demand satisfied in every period in which it is observed.
table.assumption_violation_model_non_convergen: If a model does not converge, we will in order reduce integration points, use the Laplace approximation, rescale variables, and finally fit the model in a Bayesian framework (R, brms) with weakly informative priors. Any such change will be reported.
table.reliability_and_robustness_testing: Bayesian MAIHDA. Five wealth quintiles (240 strata). Parity as a sixth dimension (432 strata). Exclusion of strata with fewer than 30 women. Restriction to married or in-union women, including ever-married surveys. Weighted multilevel models. Exclusion of surveys conducted in 2020 and 2021. Multiple imputation if exclusions exceed 5% in any survey.
table.exploratory_analyses: Any analysis not listed above will be labelled exploratory in the publication, and any change to this plan will be recorded with its date and reason in a deviations log on OSF.

text.text: Background: Demand for family planning satisfied by modern methods is Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) indicator 3.7.1, and countries have committed to universal access to family planning by 2030.
Inequalities are usually reported one social dimension at a time.
This hides how social characteristics combine and leaves open whether programmes should target social groups or strengthen services for all women.

We measured intersectional inequalities in demand satisfied by modern methods among women in sub-Saharan Africa over three decades, assessed how well social position discriminates between women, and identified groups left behind.
We did a preregistered cross-sectional analysis of 139 Demographic and Health Surveys from 38 countries with fieldwork from 1994 to 2024.
We included 675,584 women aged 15-49 years with demand for family planning and grouped them into 144 intersectional strata by age, union status, education, household wealth and residence.

We fitted multilevel logistic models with random effects for strata and surveys (multilevel analysis of individual heterogeneity and discriminatory accuracy, MAIHDA) and estimated the variance partition coefficient (VPC), the area under the curve (AUC) and the proportional change in variance (PCV).
Weighted demand satisfied rose from 27.5% in 1994-99 to 54.1% in 2018-24.

Predicted demand satisfied ranged from 13.2% (95% CI: 11.0 -15.9) among married adolescents with no schooling in the poorest rural households to 68.0% (95% CI: 63.6 -72.0) among unmarried urban women aged 25-34 years with secondary schooling in the richest households.

The strata explained only 6.9% (95% CI: 5.6 -8.7) of individual variation, with small discriminatory accuracy (AUC = 0.65; 95% CI: 0.63 -0.66), and a Bayesian model gave a similar VPC (7.0%; 95% credible interval: 5.7 -8.9).
Additive effects explained 95.1% of the betweenstratum variance.
Five strata of married rural women with no schooling were in the lowest decile in every period.
In the latest surveys, married rural women aged 15-24 years with no schooling had lower demand satisfied than other women in 29 of 30 countries (median gap 17.5 percentage points).
The 15 most disadvantaged strata held a median 16.4% of unsatisfied demand, so targeting these groups alone would reach about one in six women whose demand is not met.
The main limitations are the cross-sectional design, self-reported contraceptive use and the exclusion of 15 early surveys.
Intersectional gaps in demand satisfied by modern methods have narrowed in sub-Saharan Africa, and most of the remaining gap between groups is additive.
Social position alone discriminates poorly between women, so programmes targeted only by social group would miss most women with unmet need.
This supports strengthening universal services.

Within universal services, married adolescents and young women with no schooling in poor rural households have been left behind for three decades in almost every country and need priority, country-specific programmes if the 2030 targets are to be met.
Why was this study done?

• Sustainable Development Goal 3.7 commits countries to universal access to family planning by 2030, and the share of women whose demand is satisfied by modern methods is the main indicator of progress.
• Gaps in this indicator are usually reported by one characteristic at a time, such as age or wealth, although women live at the intersection of several characteristics.
• Programme managers need to know whether to target particular social groups or to strengthen services for all women, and which groups, if any, have been left behind.
What did the researchers do and find?

• We analysed 675,584 women with demand for family planning in 139 national surveys from 38 sub-Saharan African countries between 1994 and 2024, grouped into 144 combinations of age, marital status, schooling, wealth and residence.
• Demand satisfied ranged from 13% to 68% across groups, but group membership explained only 7% of the differences between individual women, and the gaps between groups halved over three decades.

• Married adolescents and young women with no schooling in poor rural households were among the most disadvantaged groups in every period, and in the latest surveys they lagged behind other women in 29 of 30 countries by a median of 17.5 percentage points.
• Targeting family planning programmes only by social characteristics would miss most women whose demand is not met, so universal services should remain the foundation.

• Ministries of health and FP2030 partners should give priority to married adolescents and young women with no schooling in rural areas, and should report SDG indicator 3.7.1 for this group alongside the national average.

• The study describes associations from self-reported cross-sectional survey data and cannot identify the causes of these gaps. aOR, adjusted odds ratio AUC, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve CI, confidence interval CrI, credible interval DHS, Demographic and Health Surveys ESA, east and southern Africa MAIHDA, multilevel analysis of individual heterogeneity and discriminatory accuracy MOR, median odds ratio PCV, proportional change in variance SDG, Sustainable Development Goal VPC, variance partition coefficient WCA, west and central Africa
The proportion of women whose demand for family planning is satisfied by modern methods is indicator 3.7.1 of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).
It is a core measure of progress towards universal access to sexual and reproductive health care [1] [2] [3].
text.formatted: It is a core measure of progress towards universal access to sexual and reproductive health care <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref>.

text.text: A threshold of 75% has been proposed as the level that countries should reach by 2030 [2, 4].
text.formatted: A threshold of 75% has been proposed as the level that countries should reach by 2030 <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4]</ref>.

text.text: Sub-Saharan Africa has made the largest gains of any region since the 1990s.
Yet it still has the lowest levels of demand satisfied, and progress has been uneven between and within countries [5] [6] [7] [8] [9].
text.formatted: Yet it still has the lowest levels of demand satisfied, and progress has been uneven between and within countries <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref> <ref type="bibr">[6]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref>.

text.text: The fertility transition in the region has also been slower than elsewhere [10, 11].
text.formatted: The fertility transition in the region has also been slower than elsewhere <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11]</ref>.

text.text: Studies of who is left behind usually describe gaps along one dimension at a time, such as age, wealth, residence or marital status [12, 13].
text.formatted: Studies of who is left behind usually describe gaps along one dimension at a time, such as age, wealth, residence or marital status <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13]</ref>.

text.text: In multi-country analyses, adolescents, women with no schooling, poorer women and rural women have lower demand satisfied [12, [14] [15] [16].
text.formatted: In multi-country analyses, adolescents, women with no schooling, poorer women and rural women have lower demand satisfied <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16]</ref>.

text.text: These characteristics do not occur in isolation.
A woman is not only young or poor or rural.
She may be all of them at once.
Intersectionality theory holds that social positions combine to shape access to resources and services.
The experience of people at particular intersections may therefore not be predicted by adding up single-axis disadvantages [17, 18].
text.formatted: The experience of people at particular intersections may therefore not be predicted by adding up single-axis disadvantages <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">18]</ref>.

text.text: Single-dimension analyses cannot show whether gaps combine additively or multiply.
Conventional regression with many interaction terms also becomes unstable when strata are numerous and some are small [19, 20].
text.formatted: Conventional regression with many interaction terms also becomes unstable when strata are numerous and some are small <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">20]</ref>.

text.text: Multilevel analysis of individual heterogeneity and discriminatory accuracy (MAIHDA) addresses these problems [19, 21, 22].
text.formatted: Multilevel analysis of individual heterogeneity and discriminatory accuracy (MAIHDA) addresses these problems <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">22]</ref>.

text.text: Individuals are nested in intersectional strata, and the stratum random effects give shrunken and stable estimates for every stratum.

The approach also measures how well the strata discriminate between individuals with and without the outcome, through the variance partition coefficient (VPC) and the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) [23, 24].
text.formatted: The approach also measures how well the strata discriminate between individuals with and without the outcome, through the variance partition coefficient (VPC) and the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[23,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">24]</ref>.

text.text: It separates additive effects from interaction effects [25].
text.formatted: It separates additive effects from interaction effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">[25]</ref>.

text.text: MAIHDA has been used for chronic disease, mental health and, recently, child anaemia in Latin America [24, 26].
text.formatted: MAIHDA has been used for chronic disease, mental health and, recently, child anaemia in Latin America <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[24,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">26]</ref>.

text.text: We found no published study that has applied it to demand satisfied by modern methods or to other contraceptive outcomes in sub-Saharan Africa.
Knowing which combinations of characteristics leave women behind matters for programmes.
If disadvantage is mostly additive, broad strategies that address each characteristic may be enough.
If particular combinations fare worse than expected, programmes need to be designed for them.
If social position discriminates poorly between women, targeting by social characteristics alone will miss many women in need.
These questions have not been answered for family planning in sub-Saharan Africa.
We aimed to quantify intersectional inequalities in demand satisfied by modern methods among women in sub-Saharan Africa from 1994 to 2024.
We estimated how demand satisfied varied across 144 strata defined by age, union status, education, household wealth and residence.
We assessed how much of the individual variation lay between strata and how much of it was additive.
We also examined how inequalities changed over time, how they differed between subregions and countries, and which groups were persistently left behind.
We preregistered five hypotheses.
First, demand satisfied would be lowest among adolescent, unmarried, poorer, rural women with no schooling (H1).
Second, the strata would have low to moderate discriminatory accuracy, with a VPC below 20% and an AUC below 0.70 (H2).
Third, additive effects would explain more than 80% of the between-stratum variance, with some interaction effects (H3).
Fourth, the between-stratum variance would be smaller in 2018-24 than in the 1990s, with the least improvement in strata combining adolescence, no schooling and rural residence (H4).
Fifth, inequalities would be wider in west and central Africa than in east and southern Africa (H5).
This was a preregistered cross-sectional secondary analysis of Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS).
The analysis plan was registered on OSF Registries on 19th October 2026, before any data were downloaded (doi:10.17605/OSF.IO/8M9GB; S2 Appendix).
It is reported following the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) guideline (S1 Checklist) [27].
text.formatted: It is reported following the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) guideline (S1 Checklist) <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">[27]</ref>.

text.text: DHS are nationally representative household surveys with two-stage stratified cluster sampling.
Trained interviewers administer standard questionnaires face to face [28].
text.formatted: Trained interviewers administer standard questionnaires face to face <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">[28]</ref>.

text.text: We used the women's individual recode files of all standard DHS done in sub-Saharan Africa with fieldwork from 1992 to 2024 for the 41 countries approved by the DHS Program for this project.
Interim, malaria indicator, AIDS indicator and subnational surveys were excluded.
For 30 older surveys in the main analysis whose women's file did not include wealth quintiles, we merged the DHS wealth index file through the household identifier.
This analysis used publicly available, anonymised DHS data, so no ethical approval was needed.
Access to the data was granted by the DHS Program (project 246219, 19th October 2026).
Informed consent was obtained from all respondents during the original surveys, and the authors had no contact with participants.
Of 154 eligible surveys, 13 did not measure demand for family planning among unmarried women.
These were the 12 DHS-II surveys and the 1994 survey in Côte d'Ivoire, which asked fertility preferences only of women in union [29].
text.formatted: These were the 12 DHS-II surveys and the 1994 survey in Côte d'Ivoire, which asked fertility preferences only of women in union <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">[29]</ref>.

text.text: As the protocol specifies for ever-married samples, these were used only in a sensitivity analysis of women in union.
Mozambique 2003 and Tanzania 1999 were excluded because our national estimates differed from the published values by more than 1 percentage point and the difference could not be resolved.

Chad 2004 and Niger 2006 also differed from the published values, but our estimates agreed with each survey's own unmet-need variable, so we judged the published values to be in error and retained these two surveys.
The main analysis therefore included 139 surveys from 38 countries with fieldwork from 1994 to 2024 (S1 Fig and S1 Appendix, Table S1).
text.formatted: The main analysis therefore included 139 surveys from 38 countries with fieldwork from 1994 to 2024 (S1 Fig and <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">S1</ref> Appendix, Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">S1</ref>).

text.text: These surveys interviewed 1,697,188 women aged 15-49 years, of whom 675,897 had demand for family planning.
We excluded 313 women (0.05%) with a missing stratification variable, which left 675,584 women.
Women with demand for family planning were those currently using contraception and those with unmet need for spacing or limiting, according to the revised DHS definition [29].
text.formatted: Women with demand for family planning were those currently using contraception and those with unmet need for spacing or limiting, according to the revised DHS definition <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">[29]</ref>.

text.text: Under this definition, women not in union are classified as having unmet need only if they had sexual intercourse in the four weeks before the survey, whereas women in union are classified regardless of recent sexual activity.
The outcome was coded 1 if a woman with demand was using a modern method and 0 otherwise [27].
text.formatted: The outcome was coded 1 if a woman with demand was using a modern method and 0 otherwise <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">[27]</ref>.

text.text: We used demand satisfied rather than contraceptive prevalence or unmet need because it is the SDG indicator and it compares groups with different fertility intentions on the same scale [2].
text.formatted: We used demand satisfied rather than contraceptive prevalence or unmet need because it is the SDG indicator and it compares groups with different fertility intentions on the same scale <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref>.

text.text: The revised unmet-need variable is included in the recode files of most surveys from 2010 onwards.
For the 66 earlier surveys that did not include it, we computed it with a Python translation of the DHS Program's published Stata code, including its survey-specific rules.
In 24 surveys that included the official variable, our classification agreed with it for 99.8% of women.
Demand satisfied differed by 0.2 percentage points on average (S1 Appendix, Table S2).
text.formatted: Demand satisfied differed by 0.2 percentage points on average (S1 Appendix, Table <ref type="table">S2</ref>).

text.text: We also reproduced the national estimate of demand satisfied for each survey and compared it with the published STATcompiler value.
Strata were defined by five preregistered dimensions.

These were age (15-19, 20-24, 25-34 and 35-49 years), union status (married or living with a partner, or not in union), education (none, primary, or secondary or higher), household wealth (poorest 40%, middle 20% or richest 40% of the survey's wealth index [30]) and residence (urban or rural).
text.formatted: These were age (15-19, 20-24, 25-34 and 35-49 years), union status (married or living with a partner, or not in union), education (none, primary, or secondary or higher), household wealth (poorest 40%, middle 20% or richest 40% of the survey's wealth index <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">[30]</ref>) and residence (urban or rural).

text.text: Their combination gives 144 strata, all of which were represented.
The smallest stratum had 140 women.
These dimensions are those used to monitor equity in family planning and were fixed in the protocol [12].
text.formatted: These dimensions are those used to monitor equity in family planning and were fixed in the protocol <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref>.

text.text: Religion and ethnicity were not included because their categories are not comparable across countries.
Parity was examined as a sixth dimension in a sensitivity analysis.
Weighted descriptive estimates used the DHS sampling weights, rescaled so that each survey contributed equally.
We followed the MAIHDA approach for the main models [19, 21, 22].
text.formatted: We followed the MAIHDA approach for the main models <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">22]</ref>.

text.text: Model 1 (null) was a logistic model with random intercepts for intersectional strata and, cross-classified, for surveys.
Model 2 (additive) added the main effects of the five dimensions.
From Model 1 we calculated the VPC as the stratum variance divided by the sum of the stratum variance, the survey variance and π²/3.

We calculated the AUC from predictions that included the fixed intercept and the stratum effects but not the survey effects, so that it measures the discriminatory accuracy of intersectional position alone.
We also report the median odds ratio (MOR), which expresses the stratum variance on the odds ratio scale.
It is the median odds ratio between a woman in a stratum with higher demand satisfied and a woman in a stratum with lower demand satisfied when two strata are chosen at random [23].
text.formatted: It is the median odds ratio between a woman in a stratum with higher demand satisfied and a woman in a stratum with lower demand satisfied when two strata are chosen at random <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[23]</ref>.

text.text: An AUC below 0.60 was interpreted as absent or poor discrimination, 0.60 to 0.70 as small, 0.70 to 0.80 as moderate and above 0.80 as large.
The proportional change in variance (PCV) was the reduction in stratum variance from Model 1 to Model 2.
The stratum random effects in Model 2 were interpreted as interaction effects.
They show how far a stratum departs from the prediction based on additive main effects.
An interaction effect was considered present when its 95% interval excluded zero.
Predicted probabilities for each stratum came from Model 1, with 95% intervals from 2000 simulations of the fixed intercept and the conditional distribution of the stratum effect.
Models 1 and 2 were refitted within each period, each sub-region and each country.
Sub-regions were west and central Africa (WCA) and east and southern Africa (ESA), following the UNICEF grouping.
Model 6 added random effects for stratumby-period combinations to estimate stratum trajectories.

A stratum caught up or fell further behind if its change in predicted demand satisfied from 1994-99 to 2018-24 differed from the average stratum change and the 95% simulation interval of the difference excluded zero.
Model 7 added random effects for stratum-by-country combinations.
A stratum was persistently left behind if it was in the lowest 10% of predicted demand satisfied in every period.
We checked whether the trends were driven by changes in which countries were surveyed.
We refitted the period models in the eight countries with a survey in every period and in the 11 countries with surveys in both 1994-99 and 2018-24.

To make the results usable by national programmes, we did an analysis that was not preregistered and compared weighted demand satisfied in each country's latest survey between married rural women aged 15-24 years with no schooling and all other women with demand.
This group combines the characteristics of the persistently left-behind strata.
Confidence intervals used the effective sample size, and countries with fewer than 30 women in the group were not shown.
The outcome and all stratum-defining variables are categorical.
The models were therefore fitted to binomial counts for each stratum within each survey, which gives the same likelihood as an individual-level model.
Because the counts were aggregated to strata within surveys, survey clusters could not be included as an additional level.
Models were estimated by maximum likelihood with the Laplace approximation in R version 4.3 using lme4 [31].

At country level, we examined whether between-stratum inequality was lower in countries with higher overall demand satisfied, using Spearman correlation.

text.text: These were a normal(0, 2.5) prior for the intercept and half-Student t(3, 0, 1) priors for the stratum and survey standard deviations, with four chains of 2,500 iterations including 1,000 warm-up iterations.

Mixing of the intercept was slower (R-hat 1.09), which does not affect the VPC (S1 Appendix).
We additionally excluded Chad 2004 and Niger 2006, whose published values differed from ours (see Results).
Multiple imputation was not needed because no survey had more than 5% of women excluded.
Surveys are nested in countries, and repeated surveys from one country are not independent.
We therefore fitted a three-level sensitivity model, which was not preregistered, in which strata were crossed with surveys nested in countries.
This model separates stable differences between countries from differences between surveys within a country.
We compared its VPC, PCV and interaction effects with those of the main model and tested the country variance with a likelihood ratio test.
In an exploratory analysis that was not preregistered, we examined whether factors that may lie on the pathway between social position and contraceptive use explained between-stratum differences.

These were parity, weekly exposure to mass media, hearing family planning messages, a visit from a family planning worker, being told about family planning at a health facility and current employment.
This analysis used the 105 surveys in which these variables were available for more than 90% of women.

text.text: To show what the stratum gaps mean for national coverage, we did a second exploratory analysis in the latest survey of each country.
We defined the left-behind strata as the 15 strata in the lowest 10% of predicted demand satisfied in 2018-24.
For each country we estimated their weighted share of all women with demand and their share of all women whose demand was not satisfied by modern methods.
The ratio of these shares shows whether unsatisfied demand is concentrated in these strata.
We also estimated how much national demand satisfied would rise if women in these strata had the same level as other women in that country.
We repeated this for married rural women aged 15-24 years with no schooling.
The 139 surveys included 675,584 women with demand for family planning.

Eleven of these were in the richest 40% and had started from relatively high levels.

The other three had started among the lowest and fell further behind.

Added to the additive model, they increased the explained share only from 95.1% to 95.2%.
In this preregistered analysis of 675,584 women with demand for family planning in 38 countries over three decades, demand satisfied by modern methods varied fivefold across intersectional strata.
Intersectional position, however, explained only about 7% of the individual variation and had small discriminatory accuracy.
Most of the between-stratum inequality was explained by the additive effects of age, schooling, wealth, residence and union status.
This inequality halved between 1994-99 and 2018-24, and the decline was the same in countries surveyed in every period.
These broad gains hide groups that have not benefited.
Married adolescents and young women with no schooling in poor rural households were among the lowest-ranked groups in every period.
In the latest surveys, this group lagged behind other women in almost every country.
These findings support four of our five preregistered hypotheses.
The strata had small discriminatory accuracy (H2).
Additive effects explained most of the between-stratum variance, alongside some interaction effects (H3).
Betweenstratum variance fell over time, while the poorest adolescents with no schooling improved least (H4).
Inequality was higher in west and central Africa than in east and southern Africa, although the difference was modest and the confidence intervals overlapped, so H5 was only partly supported.
H1 was supported for age, schooling, wealth and residence.
Contrary to our hypothesis, women in union, not unmarried women, had lower demand satisfied.
The narrowing of inequality is consistent with the inverse equity hypothesis.
It predicts that new interventions first reach the better off and that gaps narrow once better-off groups approach saturation [34, 35].

Rural women with primary schooling gained most.
The same pattern has been described for institutional delivery across hundreds of national surveys [35].

These data are consistent with the hypothesis but cannot prove it.
The strata that started lowest did not all follow this pattern.
Married adolescents and young women with no schooling in poor rural households stayed among the lowest-ranked strata in every period.
This suggests that general expansion of services does not resolve the mechanisms that exclude them.
Married adolescents face specific barriers.
These include provider bias, lack of privacy, pressure to prove fertility early in marriage and limited decision-making power within the household [15, 16].

text.text: Programmes designed for this group can work.
In a cluster randomised trial in Niger, a gender-synchronised programme for married adolescent girls and their husbands increased modern contraceptive use [37].

text.text: Our results suggest that such programmes are needed in almost every country in the region, not only in countries with low overall coverage.
The low discriminatory accuracy of the strata is an important result for policy.
A small VPC does not mean that the gaps between groups are unimportant.
Predicted demand satisfied still varied five-fold between strata.
It means that women within the same stratum differ greatly from each other.
An AUC of 0.65 means that knowing a woman's age, union status, schooling, wealth and residence gives only a limited indication of whether her demand is met.
Interventions targeted only by these characteristics would therefore miss many women in need while also reaching many who are already served [21, 23].

text.text: This supports universal provision of services, combined with proportionately greater effort for the most disadvantaged groups.
Survey context had more discriminatory value than intersectional position.
This points to the importance of national policy, commodity supply and health system factors [11, 38].

text.text: The large stratum-by-country variance shows that the same social position carries different risks in different countries.
National programmes therefore need to identify their own left-behind groups rather than rely on regional averages.
Our country estimates show that young married rural women with no schooling lag behind in almost every country.
This includes countries with high overall coverage such as Kenya, Sierra Leone and Mozambique, where demand satisfied among other women was above 50% and the gap was 32 to 45 points.
The gap for this group was no smaller in countries with higher overall coverage, which suggests that general expansion of services alone does not close it.
Reporting SDG indicator 3.7.1 only as a national average, or by one characteristic at a time, would miss these gaps.
Our impact analysis adds a further point.
The left-behind strata hold more than their share of unsatisfied demand, yet most women with unsatisfied demand belong to other strata.
Closing the gap for the left-behind strata alone would raise national coverage by a median of only 1.5 percentage points.
Targeted programmes for these groups are therefore needed for equity, but they cannot replace the expansion of services for all women.
This supports an approach in which services stay universal and their intensity rises with disadvantage.
Women in union had lower demand satisfied than women not in union with the same age, schooling, wealth and residence.
Unmarried women count as having demand only if they are sexually active, so they are a selected group, and many unmarried users rely on condoms and other short-acting methods [8, 13].

text.text: The restriction to women in union removes this selection, and in that analysis the VPC was 4.7%, while the AUC and the share of variance explained by additive effects were similar to the main analysis.
This finding highlights married adolescents as a group in particular need.
At the same time, the negative interaction effects among unmarried rural adolescents show that these adolescents face barriers that are not captured by the main effects.
The exploratory analysis showed that contact with family planning services, exposure to family planning messages and employment were associated with demand satisfied.
These factors, however, explained little of the difference between strata beyond the additive effects.
The disadvantage of the left-behind groups is therefore not simply due to less contact with services.
It may reflect structural and normative barriers, such as partner opposition and early marriage, that our survey variables did not capture.
The study has several strengths.
The analysis was preregistered and used standard surveys from almost all countries in the region over three decades.
We applied one definition of unmet need to every survey, rebuilt the indicator for older surveys with the DHS Program's own algorithm and validated it.
We also checked every national estimate against the published value.
MAIHDA gives stable estimates for small strata and separates additive from interaction effects.
Results were consistent across preregistered sensitivity analyses, including Bayesian estimation, and in countries surveyed in every period.
A three-level model that allowed for the nesting of surveys within countries gave the same results.
There are also limitations.
First, the analysis is descriptive and cross-sectional, and the strata are markers of social position rather than causes.
Second, the surveys included differ between periods, although the decline in between-stratum inequality was the same in the eight countries surveyed in every period.
Third, contraceptive use, union status and sexual activity are self-reported.
Use may be under-reported among unmarried women, which could bias their estimates in either direction.
Fourth, the wealth index is relative within each survey, so a wealth group does not represent the same living standard across countries or periods.
Fifth, the 13 surveys that did not measure unmet need among unmarried women and two surveys with unresolved differences from published estimates were excluded from the main analysis.
This reduced coverage of the early 1990s, although the analysis of women in union that included eight of them gave similar results.
Sixth, the interaction effects are descriptive and may partly reflect differences in composition within strata, such as parity or region.
Seventh, the main models were unweighted and did not include survey clusters as a level, although models weighted with scaled survey weights gave similar results.
As a result, differences between communities within a survey were not separated from individual variation.
The categories of each dimension were also broad, and finer categories could reveal larger gaps.
Finally, the exploratory variables were not available for all surveys and could not capture partner opposition, provider behaviour or service quality.
Intersectional inequalities in demand satisfied by modern methods have narrowed in sub-Saharan Africa, and most of the remaining gaps between groups are additive.
Social position alone discriminates poorly between women, which supports universal services.
Married adolescents and young women with no schooling in poor rural households have, however, been left behind for three decades in almost every country.
Reaching universal access by 2030 is likely to require universal services combined with country-specific programmes that reach these women.
Countries should report SDG indicator 3.7.1 by combinations of social characteristics rather than one dimension at a time.
